name: Hierarchical Latent Variable Model
analogy: Think of it as describing a trading day on two levels: a headline for the whole session, such as grinding uptrend on light volume, and the bar-by-bar details that fit under that headline. The model learns both levels from the bars alone and can write new details to fit any headline.

steps.title: Read a long stretch of bars
steps.description: The model takes a trajectory of bars, long enough to show the shape of a session or a few days. It must explain this stretch at two levels of detail at once.
steps.inExample: A window of 78 five-minute MNQ bars, one full cash session, is read in one go.

steps.title: Infer the slow, top-level code
steps.description: An inference network reads the whole window and produces a spread of values for a top-level code. This code captures what is true of the stretch overall: its general trend, volatility level and character.
steps.inExample: The top-level code lands near a grinding-uptrend, moderate-volatility character for the session.

steps.title: Infer the fast, bottom-level codes
steps.description: Given the top-level code, a second network reads short pieces of the window and produces bottom-level codes for each piece. They capture the local, bar-to-bar movements consistent with the overall character.
steps.inExample: Bottom-level codes describe pullbacks of about 15 to 25 points against the broader advance.

steps.title: Rebuild the bars from both levels
steps.description: A generator takes the top and bottom codes and rebuilds the bars. Training asks for a good rebuild while keeping both codes close to simple priors, so the codes carry useful structure and not noise.
steps.inExample: The rebuilt session shows a similar overall drift and the same typical range per bar as the real one.

steps.title: Use different clocks for the two levels
steps.description: The top-level code is set once for the whole window, while the bottom-level code changes frequently. That difference in clocks is what gives the levels their different roles.
steps.inExample: The session code stays fixed across the 78 bars, while the local code updates every 3 bars.

steps.title: Generate or compare
steps.description: To generate, fix the top-level code and sample new bottom-level codes, yielding new bar paths for that kind of session. To compare, line up top-level codes from different periods to find similar ones.
steps.inExample: With the grinding-uptrend code fixed, 100 new sessions are sampled, each with different pullbacks but the same overall character.

useFor.task: Conditioning an agent on the market's character
useFor.example: Feeding the session-level code to a high-level policy that chooses a trend or range approach, and the bar-level code to the execution policy.
Generating 100 synthetic grinding-uptrend sessions to stress-test a stop-loss rule inside that regime.
Flagging the bar where the top-level code moves sharply, such as when a quiet range turns into a news-driven selloff.
Comparing top-level codes across ES and MNQ to find days whose overall character matched.
Using the learned codes as inputs to a separate supervised or reinforcement learning model.

avoidWhen: You want a plainly named regime such as bull, bear or sideways; a hidden Markov regime model gives labelled states that are easier to read and check.
A single bar-level prediction is the goal; the two-level structure adds training effort that a direct model avoids.

example.scenario: After a full MNQ cash session of 78 five-minute bars, the model is asked to summarize the session at two levels and then to generate a fresh session of the same character.

input.summary: One window of bars from a single session.

fields.name: window length
fields.meaning: The number of bars in one full cash session.

fields.name: session open
fields.meaning: The price at the start of the window, rounded to a whole point.

fields.name: session close
fields.meaning: The price at the end of the window, rounded to a whole point.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a five-minute bar across the session.

fields.name: total volume against its 20-day average
fields.meaning: How heavy the whole session's trading was compared with the recent norm.

output.summary: The two levels of code and a generated session of the same character.

fields.name: top-level session code
fields.meaning: The slow code summarizing the session; the label was attached afterwards by inspecting similar sessions.

fields.name: bottom-level codes
fields.meaning: The fast codes describing local movement under the session code, one per 3-bar piece.

fields.name: generated session drift
fields.meaning: The overall move of a new session sampled with the same top-level code.

fields.name: generated typical pullback
fields.meaning: The typical size of dips in the generated session.

example.reading: Compare generated sessions with real ones of the same character: if drift and pullback sizes land in the same ranges, the generator is realistic enough to stress-test with. The label on the top-level code is a human interpretation added afterwards, so check it against the price chart.
